subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 27-year-old man presents with 5 days of fever, nausea, anorexia, and right upper quadrant discomfort, followed by dark urine and jaundice. ALT is 1450 U/L and bilirubin is 5.2 mg/dL. He returned 4 weeks ago from a trip to Central America and recalls eating raw shellfish at a beach restaurant. Serology is positive for IgM anti-HAV and negative for HBsAg.
question: Which of the following best explains why hepatitis A is not destroyed by gastric acid and small bowel contents?

options.text: It establishes a chronic carrier state that shields it from digestive enzymes
It is a hepadnavirus whose DNA polymerase repairs acid-induced capsid damage
It enters through the respiratory tract and only later reaches the liver hematogenously
It is an enveloped picornavirus that is stabilized by the lipid bilayer at low pH
It is a naked virus that lacks an envelope, resisting the gut, whereas hepatitis B is parenterally transmitted

explanation_correct: Hepatitis A is a naked positive-sense ssRNA picornavirus, and naked viruses are not destroyed by the gut; the mnemonic is that the vowels (A and E) hit your bowels. Its transmission is fecal-oral, classically via shellfish, contaminated water, travelers, and day care outbreaks, and it causes acute self-limited hepatitis with IgM anti-HAV as the best acute marker and no carrier state.

explanation_incorrect.A: HAV has no carrier state; chronic carriage is a feature of hepatitis B and C, not A.
explanation_incorrect.B: HAV is a picornavirus, not a hepadnavirus; HAV has no DNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase.
explanation_incorrect.C: HAV transmission is fecal-oral; respiratory spread is not a described route.
explanation_incorrect.D: HAV is nonenveloped; a lipid envelope would make it more, not less, vulnerable to acid and detergents.

educationalObjective: Hepatitis A is a naked picornavirus transmitted fecal-orally with no carrier state and no chronic disease, unlike the parenterally spread hepatitis B hepadnavirus.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 62-year-old man is seen for fatigue and mild jaundice. Laboratory studies show positive HBsAg, positive IgG anti-HBc, positive anti-HBe, and negative IgM anti-HBc. His ALT is mildly elevated. He has been followed for 3 years with persistently positive HBsAg.
question: Which of the following best interprets this serologic pattern?

options.text: Chronic hepatitis B with low transmissibility, indicated by anti-HBe positivity
Resolved hepatitis B with no residual virus
Hepatitis D superinfection with suppressed HBV markers
Acute hepatitis B in the window period, with IgM anti-HBc pending
Immunity from prior hepatitis B vaccination alone

explanation_correct: Persistent HBsAg beyond 6 months indicates chronic infection, and IgG anti-HBc confirms prior exposure; IgM anti-HBc would mark acute infection. Anti-HBe appears when HBeAg is cleared and indicates low transmissibility with a better prognosis. The HBeAg/anti-HBe axis reflects active viral replication, since HBeAg is secreted into the circulation and is not part of the mature virion.

explanation_incorrect.B: Resolved infection would show anti-HBs and anti-HBc positivity with negative HBsAg; persistent HBsAg means ongoing infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: HDV superinfection would show HDV markers such as anti-HDV; it does not produce isolated anti-HBe positivity as the explanation for chronic HBsAg carriage.
explanation_incorrect.D: During the window period HBsAg has cleared and IgM anti-HBc may be the sole marker; here HBsAg and IgG anti-HBc are both positive and the pattern has persisted for years.
explanation_incorrect.E: Vaccination produces anti-HBs without anti-HBc, because anti-HBc requires infection with intact virus, not the surface antigen vaccine.

educationalObjective: Chronic hepatitis B is defined by HBsAg positivity beyond 6 months with IgG anti-HBc; anti-HBe positivity indicates low transmissibility and a better prognosis.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 24-year-old woman who works as a nurse sustains a needlestick injury from a patient known to have chronic hepatitis B. She has no record of vaccination and her baseline serology shows negative HBsAg, negative anti-HBs, and negative anti-HBc.
question: Which of the following serologic results would document successful hepatitis B vaccination rather than natural infection?

options.text: Positive anti-HBs with negative anti-HBc
Positive anti-HBc (IgG) with negative anti-HBs
Positive HBeAg with negative anti-HBs
Positive HBsAg with positive IgM anti-HBc
Positive IgM anti-HAV with negative anti-HBs

explanation_correct: Anti-HBs indicates immunity to hepatitis B from vaccination or from recovery after infection, and it protects against reinfection. Vaccination uses surface antigen only, so anti-HBc never appears; anti-HBc requires infection with whole virus. Isolated anti-HBs therefore marks vaccine-induced immunity, whereas anti-HBs plus anti-HBc marks recovery from natural infection.

explanation_incorrect.B: Anti-HBc positivity indicates infection with intact virions rather than vaccination, and without anti-HBs this pattern suggests remote or chronic infection rather than immunity.
explanation_incorrect.C: HBeAg reflects active viral replication and high transmissibility; it is never a marker of immunity from vaccine.
explanation_incorrect.D: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc indicates acute hepatitis B infection, which is the outcome to be prevented, not evidence of protection.
explanation_incorrect.E: IgM anti-HAV is the best test for acute hepatitis A and says nothing about hepatitis B immunity.

educationalObjective: Anti-HBs alone indicates vaccine immunity, whereas anti-HBs plus anti-HBc indicates immunity from natural infection; the vaccine contains only surface antigen and never induces anti-HBc.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 30-year-old woman presents with fever, arthralgias, and a urticarial rash, followed 1 week later by jaundice. Serology shows HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative, and HBeAg positive. Liver biopsy shows hepatocytes with a granular eosinophilic ground-glass appearance.
question: Which of the following best explains the ground-glass hepatocyte appearance and the high transmissibility in this patient?

options.text: Iron deposition in periportal hepatocytes secondary to chronic hemolysis
Accumulation of hepatitis B surface antigen within infected hepatocytes, with HBeAg indicating active replication
Macrovesicular steatosis with lymphoid aggregates typical of hepatitis C
Councilman bodies from hepatocyte apoptosis, which are specific to hepatitis A
Cytopathic destruction of hepatocytes directly by HBsAg, without a T-cell response

explanation_correct: In hepatitis B, the ground-glass hepatocyte appearance results from accumulation of surface antigen within infected hepatocytes, and injury is mediated by cytotoxic T cells rather than direct cytopathic effect. HBeAg is secreted into the circulation, indicates active viral replication, and therefore predicts high transmissibility and a poorer prognosis. The serum-sickness-like prodrome of fever, arthralgias, and rash is a classic early HBV presentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Iron deposition with periportal hepatocytes describes hemochromatosis, which is unrelated to acute icteric hepatitis B.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lymphoid aggregates with focal macrovesicular steatosis describe hepatitis C histology, not the ground-glass change of hepatitis B.
explanation_incorrect.D: Councilman bodies are eosinophilic apoptotic globules seen in hepatitis A and yellow fever; they are not the ground-glass finding.
explanation_incorrect.E: HBV is not directly cytopathic; cytotoxic T cells mediate the hepatocyte damage, which is why immunosuppression can produce high viral loads with little inflammation.

educationalObjective: Ground-glass hepatocytes reflect surface antigen accumulation in hepatitis B, damage is T-cell mediated, and HBeAg marks active replication with high transmissibility.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 34-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B is evaluated for proteinuria and edema. Renal biopsy shows a membranous glomerulonephropathy pattern. He also reports episodes of myalgias and skin nodules, and biopsy of a small artery shows transmural inflammation consistent with polyarteritis nodosa.
question: Which of the following best accounts for these extrahepatic findings?

options.text: Essential mixed cryoglobulinemia due to chronic hepatitis C
Immune complex deposition associated with chronic hepatitis B
Direct cytopathic infection of renal podocytes and medium arteries by HBV
Aplastic anemia caused by parvovirus B19 coinfection
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis related to hepatitis C with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma

explanation_correct: Chronic hepatitis B is associated with membranous glomerulonephritis, which is more common than membranoproliferative GN, and with polyarteritis nodosa, a necrotizing vasculitis of medium vessels. These extrahepatic manifestations are immune complex mediated rather than a direct viral cytopathic effect. Hepatitis C shows the mirror-image pattern: membranoproliferative GN is more common than membranous and essential mixed cryoglobulinemia is classic.

explanation_incorrect.A: Essential mixed cryoglobulinemia and an increased risk of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma are hepatitis C associations, not hepatitis B.
explanation_incorrect.C: These lesions reflect circulating immune complex deposition; HBV does not directly infect podocytes or medium-sized arteries to cause this pattern.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aplastic anemia is a described hematologic manifestation of hepatitis B, but it does not explain membranous nephropathy or polyarteritis nodosa.
explanation_incorrect.E: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is listed under hepatitis C extrahepatic manifestations, along with the lymphoma risk.

educationalObjective: Hepatitis B causes membranous GN and polyarteritis nodosa by immune complex deposition, whereas hepatitis C causes membranoproliferative GN, mixed cryoglobulinemia, and B-cell lymphoma.
